title: Course final
sub: From memory fences to async locks
cards/0/q: A background thread spins while (!_stop) { … } on a plain bool field. In Release it sometimes does not stop after _stop = true. Which fix is reliable?
cards/0/options/1: Add Thread.Sleep(0) to the loop body
cards/0/options/2: Wrap only the _stop = true write in a lock
cards/0/explain: The JIT may read a plain field once and hoist the read out of the loop. Volatile.Read (or volatile on the field) forbids that. A call inside the loop merely gets in the way of one particular optimization and guarantees nothing, and a lock on one side only does not order the reads on the other.
cards/1/q: Code ran for years on x64 servers and started breaking after moving to ARM64. What could have shown up for the first time? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: Two plain writes became visible to another core in reverse order
cards/1/options/1: Two plain reads of different fields executed in reverse order
cards/1/options/2: An aligned int write stopped being atomic
cards/1/options/3: Interlocked.CompareExchange stopped being a full fence
cards/1/explain: x64 reorders only write→read, ARM64 reorders all four pairs. Atomicity of aligned writes up to pointer size and the full fence of Interlocked are guaranteed on both architectures.
cards/2/q: Add returns right away, but the total does not change. Which line is to blame?
cards/2/explain: The arguments are swapped: the new value comes first, then the expected one. Here the CAS expects current + amount in the field, which is not there — nothing is written, current is returned, and the method thinks it succeeded. Correct: CompareExchange(ref _total, current + amount, current).
cards/3/q: Put in order the path of a thread that hit a taken lock
cards/3/items/0: Try to take the lock with one CAS
cards/3/items/3: The owner leaves the lock and wakes a waiter
cards/3/items/4: The woken thread tries to take the lock again
cards/3/explain: All hybrid locks work this way: a fast path without the kernel, a little spinning, and only then an expensive sleep. A woken thread does not get the lock automatically — it competes for it again.
cards/4/explain: CS1996: await inside a lock body is forbidden — both with Monitor and with the new Lock. The lock belongs to a thread, and after await the method may continue on another one. The async lock is SemaphoreSlim with WaitAsync and Release in finally.
cards/5/q: Which primitives can be released from another thread, and so survive an await between acquire and release? Select all.
cards/5/explain: Semaphores have no owner — only a counter. Monitor, Mutex and Lock remember the owning thread and are released only by it. But only SemaphoreSlim fits async code: Semaphore has no WaitAsync, its WaitOne blocks the thread.
cards/6/q: Match the task with the tool
cards/6/pairs/0/0: A request counter from many threads
cards/6/pairs/1/0: One instance of the program per machine
cards/6/pairs/2/0: A critical section with await inside
cards/6/pairs/3/0: An expensive per-key factory in a cache
cards/6/pairs/4/0: Producer and consumer in async code
cards/7/q: WPF, a button handler calls LoadAsync().Result, and LoadAsync contains an await without ConfigureAwait(false). The window froze forever. Why?
cards/7/options/0: The continuation after await waits for the UI thread, and the UI thread is blocked in .Result waiting for the continuation
cards/7/options/1: The thread pool is exhausted, and the continuation has nowhere to run
cards/7/options/2: .Result threw an AggregateException, and the window stopped processing messages
cards/7/options/3: A Task created on the UI thread cannot be awaited from the UI thread
cards/7/explain: The classic synchronization context deadlock: two parties wait for each other, like two threads taking locks in opposite order. The cure is async all the way up; ConfigureAwait(false) in a library is the second line of defense.
cards/8/q: Which order of picking a synchronization tool makes sense?
cards/8/options/0: Ready-made high-level tools (Channel, Concurrent collections, Lazy), then lock, and only after measuring — Interlocked and volatile
cards/8/options/1: volatile on every shared field first: it is the cheapest way, everything else only when needed
cards/8/options/2: A named Mutex wherever there is shared data: it works even across processes
cards/8/options/3: SpinLock instead of lock throughout the code: it never enters the kernel and so is always faster
cards/8/explain: The lower the level, the more ways to get it wrong: volatile does not make ++ atomic, a CAS loop is easy to get backwards, SpinLock breaks when copied. High-level tools are already debugged, and an uncontended lock costs tens of nanoseconds.
